title: Targeted search: finding the clients that fit your service for Personal and fitness training
audience: Personal trainers and fitness coaches who want more work from clients that suit their service, their area and their session pattern.
learningOutcomes: Build a prospect list that is scored against written fit criteria for service area, session type and repeat need.
Identify public signals that a client need is starting, and explain why each one is a reasonable reason to make contact.
Write a first approach that makes one specific, verifiable observation, offers one small next step and can be declined easily.

instruction.heading: Decide what training work you want before you look for it
instruction.body: Targeted search starts with a clear picture of the work you want more of. Write down the session types you deliver well (one-to-one, small group or workplace programme), the price range you can sustain, the suburbs you can reach without losing money on travel, and how often each kind of client needs you. A fortnightly client on a route you already run is worth far more to a sole trainer than a single session across town. These criteria are the filter for everything that follows. Business.gov.au suggests writing one short profile for each customer segment (business.gov.au, 24 September 2024).

instruction.heading: Build a scored prospect list
instruction.body: Keep every candidate in one list with a fit column and a status column. Score each prospect as strong fit, possible fit or not a fit against written criteria. Ask whether it sits inside your service area, whether it has a repeat need, whether you can reach the person who decides, and whether the work falls within your insurance and qualifications. Workplaces with a staff wellbeing or gym-subsidy programme are a segment worth testing. Fitness Passport, a vendor, says employees pay their own memberships and employers can subsidise them, and its chief executive says some employer partners reach about 40 per cent of their workforce (AusLeisure, 17 August 2026). That is a vendor claim and has not been checked. Building managers and strata managers who look after shared amenities are another segment to test. The research did not find demand data for either segment, so score them on your own evidence. Record the date each entry was added and where its details came from. Use only contact details published for business use, and do not buy or harvest lists. ACMA says buying a list does not remove the need to show consent (ACMA, Spam Act obligations, last updated 28 March 2019).

instruction.heading: Watch for public signals, not private people
instruction.body: A signal is a public event that makes a need more likely soon. Examples include a public notice of planned building works, a new business opening on a street where you already work, a change of occupier at a site you already serve, a new office fit-out, or a competitor closing in your area. Use signals to decide when to make contact, not to build a profile of individuals. Public tender registers are useful for businesses and public bodies. In Victoria, Buying for Victoria lists current and past tenders and lets suppliers set alerts, and each agency publishes an annual plan of what it intends to buy (Buying for Victoria, last updated 7 August 2026). A council or agency tender for exercise or wellbeing programmes is the kind of notice to watch for. Some councils publish planning permit registers. The City of Casey register on Victoria's open data portal has suburb and status fields, so check your own council's register. Do not monitor private people, use personal information that is not public, or turn up at a home to make an offer.

instruction.heading: Make a first approach that is specific and easy to decline
instruction.body: A useful first message does three things. It states how you learned about the business or notice. It makes one specific observation that you can verify from public view or from the business's own published material, such as a notice about works or a published staff amenity. It then offers one small next step, such as a short written proposal for a defined set of sessions or a fifteen-minute call. Keep the message short, do not overstate what you know, and make it simple to say no. Where the message goes by email, text or another electronic channel, check the consent and unsubscribe rules first. The ACCC's 2026 review of unsolicited selling found that many approaches were pressured or misleading and that many salespeople did not identify themselves. About 80 per cent of respondents said unsolicited selling seldom gave useful information or offers, and about 71 per cent of salespeople identified themselves (ACCC, 28 July 2026). A specific, honest message that names you is therefore a practical advantage as well as a compliance step.

instruction.heading: Follow up on a fixed schedule and stop when asked
instruction.body: Decide in advance how many follow-ups you will send and how far apart they will be. One example pattern is a single reminder after a week and a final message after a further two weeks, then a pause. Stopping is part of the approach. If a prospect says no, or asks you to stop, remove them from the list at once and record the request with its date. At the end of each month, review which fit tier and which signal produced the replies that became paid work, and move your effort toward them. Silence is not consent to keep contacting someone.

procedure: Write the session types, area, price and repeat-need criteria for the work you want.
Build the prospect list and score each entry as strong fit, possible fit or not a fit, with a reason.
Choose two or three public signals to watch and note the date each one is seen.
Write one first message for each fit tier, with a stated source, one verifiable observation and one small next step.
Check each message against the electronic message rules, the Do Not Call rules and your insurance before sending.
Send to strong-fit prospects first, then follow up on the fixed schedule.
Remove anyone who asks you to stop, and review the results at the end of the month.

workedExamples.situation: A personal trainer covers three suburbs. A public notice goes up about planned repairs to the shared gym and amenities area in one building, and the strata manager's general enquiries email is published on the building's contact page.
workedExamples.decisionPrompt: Should the trainer send a sales message to the strata manager now, and what should it contain?
workedExamples.reasoning: The trainer should not send a sales email just because a general enquiries address is published. ACMA's Spam Act guidance says publishing a business address does not by itself permit commercial messages, and implied consent is narrow for a shared inbox. The trainer first checks whether the manager has invited contact or agreed to receive messages. If neither applies, the trainer waits for an invitation or uses a route the manager has agreed to. A phone call to a registered number is limited by the Do Not Call Register rules, so the trainer checks the register and the calling hours first. Any message that does go out names the notice, says how the trainer learned of it, offers one item the trainer can deliver, such as a written proposal for a limited set of sessions, and asks one question. The trainer does not contact individual owners or tenants using private details, and does not enter the shared area without an invitation.

equipmentAndPpe: Prospect list in a spreadsheet or notebook, with fit and status columns
Written fit criteria for service area, session type and repeat need
Message templates checked against the electronic message rules
No PPE is needed for desk work; any site visit follows the site's own safety rules

commonErrors.error: Sending the same message to everyone on a broad list at once.
commonErrors.prevention: Score the list first, write one message for each fit tier, and start with the strong-fit tier.

commonErrors.error: Using private information about an individual to make contact.
commonErrors.prevention: Use only contact details published for business use, or details the person has given you for this purpose.

commonErrors.error: Pitching a service that you are not insured to deliver.
commonErrors.prevention: Check your insurance and qualifications before outreach, and remove that service from the message.

commonErrors.error: Following up without a limit, or continuing after a request to stop.
commonErrors.prevention: Set a fixed number of follow-ups and a stop rule, and record every stop request.

safetyAndRegulatory.point: Do not offer a licensed or authorised service in outreach unless you hold the licence that the state or territory where the work is done requires. Personal training industry registration is optional under Better Health's guidance, but insurers and rebate schemes set their own conditions. This lesson does not grant any licence. Check the rules for each state you work in.

Commercial electronic messages, including email and text, are regulated by the Spam Act 2003 (Cth). ACMA says marketing messages need consent, that consent should be recorded, and that unsubscribe requests must be honoured within five working days (ACMA, avoid-spam guidance, no date shown). ACMA's Spam Act obligations page (last updated 28 March 2019) says the Act also covers business addresses, and that publishing an address does not by itself permit commercial messages. The Act text was not read for this lesson.

Public information does not by itself permit contact. The OAIC's guidance on direct marketing (APP 7, modified 16 October 2023; version 1.1 dated 22 July 2019) says public information is not exempt from the direct-marketing rules, if the Privacy Act applies to your business. Use only contact details published for business use, keep them secure, and stop using them when someone objects.

Telemarketing to registered numbers is limited to weekdays from 9 am to 8 pm and Saturdays from 9 am to 5 pm, and never on Sundays or public holidays, according to the Do Not Call Register industry guide (2018 copyright notice, older source). Check the current rules before calling.

qualityStandard: Every prospect on the list has a fit score, a reason for that score and a recorded source for its contact details.
Every first message contains one verifiable observation and one small, easy-to-decline next step.
No contact is made using private information, and every stop request is recorded and actioned.
documentationEvidence: Prospect list with fit score, reason, status, source and date added.
Signal log with the date each public signal was seen.
Stop-request record with the date it was actioned.
summary: Define the training work you want first, then filter prospects against that definition.
Watch public signals, and never use private information to make contact.
Keep the first approach specific and easy to decline, and stop when asked.

knowledgeChecks.question: Which prospect should you contact first?
options: A one-off job well outside your service area, because it looks large
A property group with several sites inside your service area that you already visit
Any business that has a website, because it probably spends money on services

knowledgeChecks.question: A public notice shows planned works at a building in your area. What is the most appropriate first step?
options: Contact the building's manager about the works, by a route that the electronic message and do-not-call rules allow
Message each resident using their private contact details and ask them to sign up for the works
Go into the common area to look at the work before making contact and ask the crew what they are doing

knowledgeChecks.question: Before you send a commercial email to a prospect, what should you do?
options: Check that the message is short enough to read on a phone and it has a fun subject line
Ask the prospect to like your social media page first and then send the message
Confirm the Spam Act 2003 requirements in current ACMA guidance before sending

officialReferences.title: Avoid sending spam (ACMA)
officialReferences.covers: Read 2026-11-03: a business needs consent before sending marketing messages, and consent must be recorded; each message must accurately identify the sender and include correct contact details for at least 30 days; every commercial message must include an unsubscribe option that is free, works for at least 30 days and is honoured within 5 working days. The page as read does not name the Spam Act 2003 and does not cover privacy law. Publisher: Australian Communications and Media Authority (ACMA).

officialReferences.title: Australian Privacy Principles guidelines (OAIC)
officialReferences.covers: Read 2026-11-03: the APPs and guidelines apply to organisations covered by the Privacy Act; the page states that the Act covers organisations with an annual turnover of more than $3 million and some other organisations, without listing them. The page as read lists the APP chapters but does not set out collection or consent rules; the full text is in a linked PDF that was not read, so small business coverage and consent detail are UNCONFIRMED. Publisher: Office of the Australian Information Commissioner (OAIC).
